content: C-C chemokine receptor type 10 (CCR10) is a protein encoded by the CCR10 gene in humans. Chemokines are small proteins, typically ranging from 8 to 14 kilodaltons in size, that are predominantly basic in nature and share structural similarities. These molecules are critical in regulating the movement (or trafficking) of various leukocyte subtypes by interacting with specific seven-transmembrane, G protein-coupled receptors. Beyond their role in cell trafficking, chemokines are essential for the development, maintenance (homeostasis), and proper functioning of the immune system. They also exert effects on cells within the central nervous system and influence endothelial cells, which are involved in processes such as angiogenesis (the formation of new blood vessels) or angiostasis (the inhibition of blood vessel formation). Chemokines are categorized into two primary subfamilies, CXC and CC, based on the arrangement of the first two of their four conserved cysteine residues. In CXC chemokines, the first two cysteines are separated by a single amino acid, whereas in CC chemokines, these cysteines are adjacent to one another. CCR10 is a receptor for chemokines, and its known ligands are CCL27 and CCL28. This receptor is typically expressed by melanocytes, plasma cells, and T cells that are directed to the skin (skin-homing T cells). Experimental studies have shown that when CCR10 is introduced into B16 melanoma cells, it significantly enhances the development of lymph node metastases in mice following skin inoculation. This finding suggests that CCR10 plays a role in guiding metastatic processes. Additionally, interactions between CCR10 and its ligand CCL27 are implicated in T cell-mediated inflammatory responses in the skin.
